title: Feature Scaling & Transforms
html:
Scaling puts features on comparable ranges. It matters for models that use distances, dot products or gradient descent, and not at all for tree-based models.

ScalerFormulaResultUse when
StandardScalerz = (x − mean) / stdMean 0, std 1 (unbounded)Default for linear models, SVM, PCA, k-NN, neural nets
MinMaxScaler(x − min) / (max − min)Range [0, 1]Bounded inputs needed (pixel values); no big outliers
RobustScaler(x − median) / IQRMedian 0, IQR 1Outliers present
MaxAbsScalerx / max(|x|)Range [−1, 1], keeps zerosSparse data
NormalizerEach row divided by its normEvery row has length 1Text vectors / cosine similarity — not a per-feature scaler

Why it matters: k-NN on the wine data

Two of the 13 wine features (magnesium, proline) have far larger numbers than the rest, so they dominate Euclidean distance until everything is standardised:

Needs scalingDoesn't need scaling
k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, linear/logistic regression with regularisation, anything trained by gradient descent (including neural nets)Decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, Naive Bayes (each feature handled separately)

Fit on train, transform everything

Do

Fit the scaler on the training data (inside a Pipeline for cross-validation) and use transform on validation/test/production data.

Avoid

fit_transform on the whole dataset before splitting, or re-fitting on the test set — both leak or shift information.

Transforming skewed features

Watch out

Standardising changes the scale, not the shape: a skewed feature stays skewed with mean 0 and std 1. Use a log / Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson transform (or QuantileTransformer) to change the shape.

Normalization vs standardization?

Min-max normalization maps a feature to [0, 1] using its min and max — sensitive to outliers. Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation — unbounded, usually a safer default. Both are fitted on the training data. (Confusingly, sklearn's Normalizer does something else: it scales each row to unit length.)

Does a random forest need feature scaling?

No. Trees split on thresholds of one feature at a time, and any monotonic rescaling leaves the ordering — and therefore the splits — unchanged.
